chemicals.concentration_notes: ◦ Concentration: In Capsicum annuum, solanine-type glycoalkaloids are confined to the foliage (leaves and stems) at low levels. The edible fruit is not a significant source — its characteristic alkaloid is capsaicin, not solanine. Ripe bell pepper flesh is essentially non-toxic.
chemicals.description: ◦ Effect in edible peppers: At the low foliage levels present in Capsicum annuum, solanine acts mainly as a local gastrointestinal irritant, contributing to vomiting and diarrhea if green parts are chewed. The systemic neurological and cardiac effects of severe solanine poisoning are associated with high-glycoalkaloid nightshades such as Solanum pseudocapsicum, not with edible peppers, which are not likely to be lethal to cats.
chemicals.name: Solanine (foliage glycoalkaloid)

chemicals.concentration_notes: ◦ Concentration: Found primarily in the mature fruits (the peppers themselves)512. ◦ Potency: Toxicity varies by the "spiciness" of the pepper. Spicy chili and ornamental peppers are particularly dangerous due to higher capsaicin content, while mild bell peppers are considered "rather harmless" but still not recommended for feeding.
chemicals.description: ◦ Mucosal Irritation: Capsaicin is a potent irritant to mucous membranes. Upon contact or ingestion, it causes an intense burning sensation, hypersalivation (drooling), coughing, and watering of the eyes911. ◦ Gastrointestinal Distress: It irritates the gastrointestinal tract, leading to gastroenteritis, vomiting, and diarrhea.
chemicals.name: Capsaicin (or Capsaicinoids)

chemicals.name: Scopoletin

description: Bell peppers, chili peppers, and ornamental peppers all belong to the Capsicum annuum species of the nightshade family (Solanaceae). For cats, edible peppers are a mild gastrointestinal irritant rather than a serious systemic toxin — ingestion is not likely to be life-threatening. Ripe bell pepper flesh is essentially non-toxic and considered "rather harmless," though it is still not recommended as a regular food. Spicy chili and ornamental peppers contain capsaicin, the compound that makes them hot; it is a potent irritant to the mucous membranes, eyes, skin, and gastrointestinal tract, causing drooling, vomiting, and diarrhea on contact or ingestion. The plant's foliage (leaves and stems) contains low levels of solanine-type glycoalkaloids, which add to the stomach upset if chewed. Note: this entry covers true edible Capsicum annuum and should not be confused with Solanum pseudocapsicum (Jerusalem cherry), a distinct, genuinely toxic nightshade sometimes sold as "ornamental pepper."
name: Bell Pepper / Chili Pepper / Ornamental Pepper
safetyNotes: Capsaicin (chili peppers): Causes immediate drooling, coughing, gastroenteritis, tearing, and eye irritation on contact with mucous membranes.

Solanine (foliage — leaves and stems): Low levels of glycoalkaloids in the green parts can add to stomach upset (vomiting, diarrhea) if chewed. Edible pepper fruit is not a significant source and is not expected to cause tremors, heart-rhythm changes, or other systemic poisoning in cats.
Safest approach: Keep all pepper plants out of reach. If offering ripe bell pepper flesh as a very occasional treat, remove all seeds and offer only a tiny amount.

symptoms.name: Vomiting, Diarrhea, and Hypersalivation (Drooling)
symptoms.notes: The main effect of edible peppers in cats. Capsaicin in spicy peppers causes an immediate burning sensation that can lead to drooling and vomiting; low-level solanine in chewed foliage adds mild irritation to the stomach and intestinal lining. Generally self-limiting and not life-threatening.

symptoms.name: Abdominal Pain (Colic)
symptoms.notes: A cat may show a tense abdominal wall or vocalize pain upon palpation. This can follow the initial vomiting phase.

symptoms.name: Burning sensation, Coughing, Watery Eyes
symptoms.notes: Specific to capsaicin found in chili and ornamental peppers. Contact can cause conjunctivitis (eye irritation), and inhalation or swallowing can trigger a cough reflex and intense burning of the mouth and throat.

treatments.description: If the ingestion was recent (typically within 1–2 hours) and the cat is stable, the veterinarian may induce vomiting using medication (such as xylazine) to remove the plant material from the stomach. Alternatively, gastric lavage (stomach pumping) may be performed under anesthesia to wash out the stomach contents.
treatments.name: Gastrointestinal Decontamination (Emesis or Gastric Lavage)
treatments.notes: This is the primary defense to prevent toxin absorption. Do not attempt to induce vomiting at home, as this can cause further injury or aspiration. This step is usually skipped if the cat is already vomiting severely or is neurologically unstable.

treatments.description: Administration of medical-grade activated charcoal (1–4 g/kg) into the digestive tract. This substance binds to the remaining toxins (solanine/glycoalkaloids) in the gut, preventing them from entering the bloodstream.
treatments.name: Toxin Adsorption (Activated Charcoal)
treatments.notes: Because solanine can undergo "enterohepatic recirculation" (where it is reabsorbed by the body), multiple doses of charcoal may be given every 4–6 hours. A cathartic (medication to speed up bowel movements) is often given with the first dose to help expel the bound toxins.

treatments.description: The administration of crystalloid fluids directly into the vein (IV) to rehydrate the cat and maintain electrolyte balance.
treatments.name: Fluid Therapy (Intravenous Fluids)
treatments.notes: This is critical for two reasons: 1) To replace fluids lost through the severe vomiting and diarrhea caused by both solanine and capsaicin.

treatments.description: Using specific medications to treat symptoms as they arise. Atropine may be used to treat slow heart rate (bradycardia) or other cholinergic neurological signs. Antiemetics (to stop vomiting) and gastroprotectants are used to soothe the stomach lining.
treatments.name: Symptomatic Drug Therapy (Atropine & Gastroprotectants)
treatments.notes: While there is no specific antidote for solanine, atropine can counteract some of its neurological effects.
